title: Signature Key-and-Address Atlas
body:
The Signature Key-and-Address Atlas is Manon's original design for a first map of wallets: private keys never shared, public addresses shareable, signing as proof, and recovery phrases stored offline. Its premise is that newcomers need a map before they need a manual, and a map that fits on one page is used while a manual gathers dust.

The design treats the first lesson as cartography: show the territory, name its parts, and only then travel.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature wallet atlas for newcomers. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Map the private key as never-shared
  2. Map the public address as shareable
  3. Map signing as proof without showing the key
  4. Map recovery phrases to offline storage only
  5. Practice on an unimportant wallet before any real use

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Private key mapped as secret; OK :: Address mapped as shareable; OK :: Signing mapped as proof; OK :: Recovery mapped offline; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The atlas is a teaching design, not a wallet, and it does not recommend any particular wallet. Its value is the mental model it leaves behind: keys, addresses, signing, recovery. A common mistake is handing a newcomer a manual when a map would have sufficed. title: Signature Two-Keys Story
body:
The Signature Two-Keys Story is Manon's original design for teaching key pairs as a story: a public padlock anyone may close, and a private key only its owner holds. The story's rule is absolute: anyone asking for the private key is a threat, without exception, including anyone claiming to help. Its premise is that a story remembered under pressure beats a definition forgotten under pressure.

The design exists because definitions fail under pressure, while stories survive it.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature two-keys story for key pairs. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Tell the padlock story: public closes, private opens
  2. Teach that signatures prove key use without showing the key
  3. Teach that private keys live on the owner's device and backup only
  4. Teach the absolute rule: no one legitimate asks for a private key
  5. Test the story by asking who the villain is in a sample message

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: MATCH :: Public padlock shared (public vs public); MATCH :: Private key secret (secret vs secret); MATCH :: Signature proves use (proved vs proved); MATCH :: Asker is a threat (threat vs threat); matching: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all values match. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The story simplifies real cryptography and does not detail algorithms or key formats. It teaches the mental model and the absolute rule, which are what everyday safety actually requires. A common mistake is teaching key pairs as mathematics first, which newcomers forget before they need it. title: Signature Public Ledger Map
body:
The Signature Public Ledger Map is Manon's original design for a map of shared ledgers: many copies, linked entries, agreed rules, and permanence. Its central warning is drawn in the map's margin: what is written here is public and hard to remove, so the map is consulted before writing, not after. Its premise is that a map with a warning in its margin prevents more mistakes than a warning delivered after the mistake.

The design puts permanence on the map itself, because permanence is the fact newcomers most need to see first.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature shared-ledger map. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Map many copies held by many participants
  2. Map linked entries forming a history
  3. Map agreement rules deciding which entries count
  4. Mark the margin warning: public and hard to remove
  5. Consult the map before writing anything personal

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Copies mapped; OK :: Linking mapped; OK :: Agreement mapped; OK :: Permanence warning on the map; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The map teaches the shared-ledger idea, not any particular chain, whose rules, speed, and cost differ. It does not cover investment or trading, which are outside its purpose. A common mistake is explaining ledgers without ever mentioning permanence, which is their most consequential property. title: Signature Self-Held Credential Wallet
body:
The Signature Self-Held Credential Wallet is Manon's original design for a wallet where credentials live with the person they describe. Issuers give credentials to the wallet, holders show them where needed without asking the issuer, and only the claim asked for is shown. Its premise is that identity should be presented, not requested, and that the issuer should not learn where a credential was shown.

The design shifts identity from permission to proof, and proof held by the person it describes.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature self-held credential wallet design. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Receive credentials from issuers into the wallet
  2. Hold them with the person, not only with the issuer
  3. Show them where needed without asking the issuer
  4. Show only the claim asked for
  5. Honor revocation: a withdrawn credential is not presented as current

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Issuance to wallet; OK :: Holding with the person; OK :: Presentation without issuer; OK :: Minimization practiced; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The wallet is a design, not a deployed product, and credential acceptance varies by place and use. It does not promise acceptance anywhere, and it teaches the model, not any particular format. A common mistake is designing a wallet that reports every presentation back to the issuer, which defeats its purpose. title: Signature Credential Seal
body:
The Signature Credential Seal is Manon's original design for a seal that makes a claim checkable: the issuer's signature, the holder's presentation, and the verifier's check, with selective presentation built in. A verifier checks the seal without contacting the issuer, and a holder shows a threshold claim, such as over an age, without revealing a birth date. Its premise is that proof without oversharing is the whole point of a credential.

The design treats selectivity as the seal's essential feature, not as an optional extra.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature verifiable-credential seal design. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Define the three roles: issuer, holder, verifier
  2. Seal claims with the issuer's signature
  3. Let verifiers check the seal without contacting the issuer
  4. Let holders show one claim without the whole record
  5. Honor expiry and revocation as part of the seal

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Three roles defined; OK :: Issuer signature sealed; OK :: Verifier check without issuer; OK :: Selective presentation built in; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The seal is a design, not a standard, and credential formats and acceptance are still developing. It does not promise acceptance by any verifier, and it teaches the model and the selectivity habit. A common mistake is designing a credential that must be shown whole, which surrenders its privacy advantage. title: Signature Recovery Guardians
body:
The Signature Recovery Guardians is Manon's original design for recovery arranged before loss: trusted guardians chosen by the holder, a recovery phrase stored offline, and a test recovery on an unimportant wallet. Its premise is that self-held access without a reset button must have guardians, because freedom without a recovery plan is a single accident away from total loss.

The design treats guardians as the reset button that self-held systems lack, chosen by the holder rather than by a company.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature guardian recovery design. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Choose guardians while the holder can still choose
  2. Store the recovery phrase offline, never in messages or photos
  3. Test recovery on an unimportant wallet
  4. Review guardians whenever devices or relationships change
  5. Never share the phrase with a guardian who only needs to approve, not to hold

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Guardians chosen in advance; OK :: Phrase stored offline; OK :: Test recovery done; OK :: Guardians reviewed on change; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The guardians design is a plan, not a guarantee, since recovery methods differ between systems and some offer none. It does not recommend any particular method for high-value holdings, which need dedicated advice. A common mistake is assuming a company can reset a self-held wallet after loss. title: Signature Wallet Choice Compass
body:
The Signature Wallet Choice Compass is Manon's original design for choosing between custodial and self-held wallets by pointing at the trade: custodial ease and recoverability against dependence, self-held independence against finality of loss. Its premise is that there is no universally best wallet, only a wallet whose trade fits the use, and a compass that names the trade prevents popularity from deciding.

The design replaces popularity with a named trade, because a trade named is a trade chosen deliberately.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature wallet-choice compass. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Define the wallet's use before choosing
  2. Weigh custodial ease and recovery against dependence
  3. Weigh self-held independence against finality of loss
  4. Learn with small, unimportant use first
  5. Review the choice as the use grows

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Use defined; OK :: Custodial trade weighed; OK :: Self-held trade weighed; OK :: Small-scale learning first; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The compass is a decision aid, not financial advice, and it does not recommend any wallet or company. Offerings and risks change, and current terms should be read for any service considered. A common mistake is choosing by popularity without asking who holds the keys. title: Signature Approval Stamp
body:
The Signature Approval Stamp is Manon's original design for a stamp that is applied only after reading: the exact action, amount or permission, and recipient, each checked against intent. Its premise is that a signature is an approval, and an approval given blindly is the most common Web3 loss, so the stamp's rule is to refuse what cannot be read, without exception and without hurry.

The design treats unreadable signing requests as unsigned, because a signature on what was not read is not consent.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature signing-approval stamp. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Read action, amount or permission, and recipient
  2. Refuse requests that cannot be read clearly
  3. Refuse signing under time pressure from strangers
  4. Check the request against actual intent
  5. Note significant signatures with dates

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Request read fully; OK :: Unreadable refused; OK :: Time-pressure refused; OK :: Signatures noted; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The stamp is a habit, not a reading of any particular signature format, which differs between systems. Its strength is refusal: what cannot be understood is not signed. A common mistake is signing to dismiss a popup. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Signature Token Ownership Card
body:
The Signature Token Ownership Card is Manon's original design for a card stating what a token actually is: a ledger entry plus a shared understanding, with the entry distinct from any image or file it points to. Its premise is that most token confusion comes from mistaking the entry for the thing, and a card that states the distinction prevents the mistake.

The design exists because an entry is not the thing it pictures, and forgetting that is expensive.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature token-ownership card. Follow these steps in order:

  1. State that owning means controlling the key
  2. State that meaning depends on issuer and community recognition
  3. Distinguish the entry from any pointed-to file
  4. Ask what happens if the issuer or platform disappears
  5. Verify issuer and terms before trusting any claim

title: Signature Terms-Code Reader
body:
The Signature Terms-Code Reader is Manon's original design for reading a smart contract's terms before interacting: what the code does, who can change it, and what cannot be undone. Its premise is that code that runs itself is a promise that cannot be renegotiated, so its terms deserve more reading, not less, and a marketing description is never a substitute for the code's actual behavior.

The design treats code as terms, and terms as things to be read before they are agreed to by interaction.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature smart-contract terms reader. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Read what the code does, not only its description
  2. Find who can change the contract and under what rules
  3. Note what cannot be undone once run
  4. Interact only where terms and risks are understood
  5. Record the contract and the date of interaction

title: Signature Web3 Lure Spotter
body:
The Signature Web3 Lure Spotter is Manon's original design for spotting lures by their shape, not their story: fake support asking for phrases, imitation sites, send-first giveaways, and broad-permission signing requests. Its premise is that stories change while shapes repeat, so a spotter trained on shapes catches new stories, while a spotter trained on stories misses them.

The design trains shape recognition, because lures change their stories faster than their shapes.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature web3 lure spotter. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Spot fake support asking for phrases or keys
  2. Spot imitation sites through trusted channels, not sent links
  3. Spot send-first giveaways as a shape, not a story
  4. Spot broad-permission signing requests and refuse them unread
  5. Report suspected lures through the platform

Use and limits. The spotter teaches recognition, not recovery of lost funds, which is often impossible and needs prompt reporting. It does not cover investment fraud law, which varies by jurisdiction. A common mistake is believing a scam is obvious and therefore cannot catch a confident person. title: Signature Revocation Switch
body:
The Signature Revocation Switch is Manon's original design for a switch that turns a credential off: issuers maintain status that verifiers check, holders stop presenting revoked credentials, and possession alone never counts as validity. Its premise is that a credential's power lives in its status, and a system without a working switch has no way to correct a mistake or a theft.

The design treats revocation as the system's conscience: without it, every issuance is forever.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature credential revocation switch. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Maintain status that verifiers actually check
  2. Teach holders that possession is not validity
  3. Stop presenting credentials known to be revoked
  4. Ask verifiers which status sources they check
  5. Record revocations with dates and reasons

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Status maintained; OK :: Possession distinguished from validity; OK :: Revoked not presented; OK :: Verifier status sources asked; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The switch is a design, not any particular registry, and revocation systems differ in speed, privacy, and completeness. A verifier that skips status checks undermines the switch, which the design notes honestly. A common mistake is presenting a revoked credential because the file is still in the wallet. title: Signature Ledger Privacy Veil
body:
The Signature Ledger Privacy Veil is Manon's original design for a veil, not a wall, around public-ledger use: restraint in what is written, separation of addresses by purpose, and the assumption that everything on a public ledger is public forever. Its premise is that pseudonymity slips once and then the whole history wears a name, so the veil must be worn before writing, not after.

The design is honest that it is a veil: it softens recognition, it does not erase the ledger.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature ledger-privacy veil. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Assume every entry is public forever
  2. Treat addresses as pseudonyms, not anonymity
  3. Separate addresses by purpose
  4. Write no personal details to public ledgers
  5. Assume patterns can identify a person

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Public-forever assumed; OK :: Pseudonymity distinguished; OK :: Addresses separated; OK :: Personal details withheld; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The veil is a set of habits, not a privacy technology, and no record here promises unrecognizability. Privacy techniques exist and are developing, but none makes a public ledger private by default. A common mistake is believing an unnamed address is anonymous. title: Signature One-Credential Passport
body:
The Signature One-Credential Passport is Manon's original design for a passport that carries one claim across many verifiers, with separation where correlation is a concern: one credential where the same claim is genuinely needed, separate credentials where purposes differ, and only the asked claim shown each time. Its premise is that convenience that links everything is also a profile, so the passport is stamped selectively.

The design treats a passport as a set of pages, shown one at a time, not as a book handed over whole.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature cross-service credential passport. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Use one credential where the same claim is genuinely needed
  2. Use separate credentials where purposes differ
  3. Show only the claim asked for
  4. Track where each credential was presented
  5. Replace credentials whose use has grown too broad

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Shared claims identified; OK :: Separate credentials for purposes; OK :: Selective presentation practiced; OK :: Presentations tracked; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The passport is a design, not a promise of acceptance, since cross-service acceptance is still uneven. It teaches the trade between convenience and correlation for each use. A common mistake is using one credential for everything because it is convenient. title: Signature Everyday Web3 Test
body:
The Signature Everyday Web3 Test is Manon's original design for a test applied before any Web3 use: what does the task need, does a shared ledger genuinely improve the proof, do self-held credentials reduce disclosure, and does the ordinary alternative fit better. Its premise is that the right question is never whether Web3 is good, but whether it fits this task better than the ordinary alternative, and a test that asks that question prevents novelty from deciding.

The design replaces enthusiasm with a test, because enthusiasm chooses technology while a test chooses fitness.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature everyday-web3 fitness test. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List the task's needs: proof, recovery, reversibility, privacy
  2. Test whether a ledger genuinely improves proof
  3. Test whether credentials reduce disclosure
  4. Test whether automatic terms help or hinder
  5. Choose the ordinary alternative when it fits better

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: PASS score=4 threshold=4 :: Needs listed; PASS score=3 threshold=3 :: Ledger benefit tested; PASS score=3 threshold=3 :: Credential benefit tested; PASS score=3 threshold=3 :: Ordinary alternative considered; passing: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all scores at threshold. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. The test is a judgment framework, not a recommendation for any task or technology. It does not cover financial decisions, and its examples are illustrative, not assessments of any live service. A common mistake is choosing Web3 because it is new, when an ordinary account fits better. title: Signature Future Identity Charter
body:
The Signature Future Identity Charter is Manon's original design for a charter written while the holder can still decide: guardians chosen, inheritance instructions kept with a will, credential fates decided, and executors told where instructions live without keys inside them. Its premise is that identity outlives its holder's ability to manage it, so its future must be arranged while management is still possible.

The design treats a charter as a letter to the future, written by the only person who can still write it.

Signature design doctrine. Every Signature design in this pair follows three rules: the user holds the keys, so no design depends on a single company keeping them; recovery is designed before loss, not after it; and a credential's power is limited by design, so one credential never unlocks everything, and a compromised credential can be revoked.

The working method is Signature future-identity charter. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Choose guardians while the holder can choose
  2. Write inheritance instructions alongside a will
  3. Decide which credentials expire, transfer, or are destroyed
  4. Tell executors where instructions live, without keys inside
  5. Review the charter when guardians, devices, or holdings change
